Hormuz Has Terms and Conditions

Iran says the Strait of Hormuz stays closed until Washington meets Tehran’s seven conditions under the Islamabad memorandum. 

Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf said Iran will not set national security policy by “posts on X by U.S. officials.” 

Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Tehran’s plan could reopen the passage within seven days, if the United States accepts Iran’s terms. 

The American proposal reportedly returned to Iran through Qatari mediators with its usual center of gravity, nuclear limits first, everything else later. 

Tehran’s answer is that the nuclear file is not even on the table yet. Iran wants sanctions relief, an end to hostilities, release of frozen funds and the lifting of what it calls a naval blockade before it restores the shipping lane that carries roughly a fifth of seaborne oil.

That is how negotiation works when one side has a strait and the other has an aircraft carrier. Washington calls Hormuz freedom of navigation. Tehran calls it collateral. 

Trump has now repeated his ultimatum three times since the UN General Assembly. “Iran has been decimated,” he told reporters. “The only question is, it’ll either be the easy way or the hard way.” He has a decision to make, he says. Tehran hears a military threat dressed as customer service. 

The waterway is not merely closed in speeches. UK Maritime Trade Operations reported a commercial tanker struck by an unknown projectile inside the Strait, damaging its engine room. 

Its crew was safe, but the message was delivered: every stalled negotiation now has a hull attached to it. 

Meanwhile, Israel has reportedly warned Germany that Iran may target U.S. bases at Ramstein and Spangdahlem, alongside earlier warnings about RAF Fairford in Britain. 

Iran is telling the regional states not to allow their territory to serve as launchpads for U.S. or Israeli operations. 

The war is expanding by logistics map: ports, bases, airspace and shipping lanes first; declarations later. 

Trump offers Iran an easy way or a hard way. Iran offers seven conditions. The tanker takes the third option: the engine room.

The Superintelligence Committee

Trump has assigned America’s AI future to the intelligence chief. Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton will lead the White House’s new Super Intelligence Force, a 120-day task force to identify artificial intelligence’s risks and rewards, assess the federal government’s role and recommend what Washington should do. 

Clayton’s official mission is to keep the United States ahead in “superintelligence” while serving the interests of Americans. 

The term is Trump’s preferred replacement for artificial intelligence, because apparently the machines needed a bigger campaign logo before they could threaten civilization. 

The group will review reports of model breaches, cyberattacks, jailbreaks and other AI failures. 

Its charter calls for plans to respond to systemic threats while avoiding “overregulation” and “regulatory capture” that could hurt innovation and competition. 

Washington is asking how to stop a technology from destabilizing society without inconveniencing the companies building it. 

The choice of Clayton says everything. Advanced AI is no longer merely a software industry, a labor-market problem or a consumer-product controversy. 

The White House has put the spy chief in charge because it sees AI as a national-security system with a chatbot interface.

The companies call it innovation. Workers call it job loss. Security officials call it an attack surface. 

Trump calls it superintelligence. In 120 days, the task force will tell the government who is supposed to be in charge. The answer will probably be everyone who already owns the servers.
